Body: The `return` inside this `finally` block will swallow any exception thrown in the `try` (including failed `expect(...)` assertions) when `prev` is defined, causing the test to incorrectly pass. Restore `auth.json` without returning from `finally` (e.g., use an `else` branch) so failures still propagate.

The new test verifies that project-level `commands/` is loaded, but it doesn't cover the precedence rules described in the PR (e.g., `commands/` overriding `command/`, and project-level commands vs `.opencode/commands` collisions). Adding an explicit collision/precedence test would help prevent regressions and validate deterministic load order.

This adds project-level command loading, but the PR description also claims deterministic singular/plural precedence via sequential scans. `loadCommand()` still uses a brace-expanded glob (`{command,commands}/**/*.md`), and `glob` traversal order is not guaranteed, so collisions between `command/foo.md` and `commands/foo.md` can still resolve unpredictably. Consider scanning `command/` then `commands/` explicitly (and/or sorting matches) before merging to guarantee precedence.

The bash guard checks are matching the entire command string against path-based regexes (e.g., `has(cmd, sec)` / `cfg.some(rule.test(cmd))`). This won’t match common cases like `cat .env` or `rm eslint.config.js` because the protected filename is preceded by a space, so shell access/mutation to protected files and config can slip through.

Consider parsing shell arguments (or at least matching `(^|\s|/)` boundaries) and checking each path token, so commands like `cat .env` and `rm .opencode/guardrails/state.json` are reliably blocked.

`process.chdir(process.env.OPENCODE_ORIGINAL_CWD)` can throw (e.g., if the directory was deleted or the env var is malformed). Since this runs at module init time, it can crash the CLI before error handling/logging is set up.

Wrap this in a try/catch (and optionally validate the path exists) so the CLI can continue with the current CWD or emit a controlled error.

The managed deployment instructions include an absolute local filesystem path (`/Users/.../packages/guardrails/managed/opencode.json`). This won’t be valid for other developers or in the repo on CI.

Use a repository-relative path (e.g. `packages/guardrails/managed/opencode.json`) or a URL within the repo instead.

The new route-level `directory` override is persisted to the session, but the value is taken directly from the query string rather than the already-canonicalized `Instance.directory` that `WorkspaceRouterMiddleware` computes for routing. This can lead to sessions storing a different path representation than the active instance (e.g., relative paths, unnormalized casing on Windows, or paths with `..`). Prefer resolving the incoming directory (or using `Instance.directory`) before passing it to `Session.create`.

The query validator is defined as `z.object({ directory: z.string().optional() }).optional()`. Since the object already has only-optional fields, making the entire query object optional is redundant and makes `c.req.valid("query")` typed as possibly `undefined`, which complicates downstream handling. Prefer a non-optional object schema here (consistent with the other query validators in this file) and treat the validated query as `{ directory?: string }`.

`directory()` still derives the cache path from the raw `pkg` spec. Even with the win32 character replacement, specs like `acme@file:../x`, `acme@git+https://...`, or any string containing path separators / `..` can cause nested paths and can escape `Global.Path.cache/packages` via `..` or an absolute path segment. This is both a security issue (path traversal) and a reliability issue (very deep/long paths). Suggestion: use a stable encoding that cannot introduce path separators (e.g., `Hash.fast(pkg)` or base64url of the spec) as the directory name on all platforms, and optionally persist the original spec inside that directory for debugging.

Variable name `lastAt` is now misleading: the code uses `spec.indexOf("@", 1)` (first "@" after the initial character) rather than the last "@". Consider renaming to something like `sepAt` / `versionAt` to match the actual behavior and reduce confusion when maintaining this parser.
```suggestion
  const versionAt = spec.indexOf("@", 1)
  const pkg = versionAt > 0 ? spec.substring(0, versionAt) : spec
  const version = versionAt > 0 ? spec.substring(versionAt + 1) : "latest"
```

On Windows, this command’s keybind can still be matched by the global command key handler (which calls evt.preventDefault() before invoking onSelect). Because onSelect returns early, a user-configured `terminal_suspend` binding (e.g. legacy `ctrl+z`) becomes a no-op that still swallows the keystroke, preventing prompt undo or other handlers from seeing it. Consider disabling the command entirely on win32 (e.g. `enabled: process.platform !== "win32"` and/or omit its keybind) so the key event isn’t consumed, and keep the runtime guard as a safety net.

This introduces Windows-specific defaulting for `terminal_suspend`/`input_undo`, but there doesn’t appear to be a unit test covering the win32 branch (the repo already has extensive `TuiConfig` tests). Adding a test that stubs `process.platform` to `"win32"` and asserts `terminal_suspend` resolves to `none` and `input_undo` includes `ctrl+z` would help prevent regressions.

On win32, `terminal_suspend` is disabled in `app.tsx` (enabled: false), so there is no keybind conflict with `input_undo`. With the current logic, if a user explicitly sets `keybinds.terminal_suspend` (e.g. `"alt+z"` or even `"ctrl+z"`) and does not set `input_undo`, `input_undo` will default to `"ctrl+-,super+z"` and Ctrl+Z ends up unbound (no suspend, no undo). Consider treating `terminal_suspend` as effectively `none` on win32 (at least when it contains `ctrl+z`), and/or always including `ctrl+z` in the default `input_undo` binding on win32 unless the user explicitly overrides `input_undo`.
```suggestion
        result.input_undo = "ctrl+z,ctrl+-,super+z"
```

The Windows-specific `input_undo` default is hard-coded as "ctrl+z,ctrl+-,super+z", which duplicates the base default defined in `Config.Keybinds` (currently "ctrl+-,super+z"). To avoid drift if the canonical default changes, consider deriving this value from the schema/defaults (e.g., take the parsed default for `input_undo` and add `ctrl+z`).
```suggestion
      if (!keybinds.input_undo) {
        const defaultInputUndo = Config.Keybinds.parse({}).input_undo
        keybinds.input_undo = unique(["ctrl+z", ...defaultInputUndo.split(",")]).join(",")
      }
```

`hooks` is defined twice at the top level. In JSONC/JSON the later key wins, so the `guardrails.sh` PreToolUse hook will be silently overridden and never run. Combine these entries under a single `hooks.PreToolUse` array (or merge by event) so both hooks are applied.

This workflow was switched to `pull_request_target` while also checking out and executing the PR’s head SHA. That combination runs untrusted PR code with the base-repo token/permissions context, which is a common secret-exfiltration vector. Use `pull_request` for tests/typecheck, or keep `pull_request_target` but only run trusted code (e.g., checkout base ref and avoid executing PR scripts).
```suggestion
  pull_request:
```

`name: unit-${{ matrix.settings.name }}-...` still references `matrix.settings.name`, but this job no longer defines a matrix. That will resolve to an empty/undefined context and can fail or produce confusing artifact names. Update this to a concrete value (e.g., `unit-linux-...`) or reintroduce the matrix.

Same concern as `test.yml`: using `pull_request_target` while checking out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` runs untrusted PR code with base-repo token/permissions context. Prefer `pull_request` for typechecking, or ensure the workflow does not execute PR-controlled code when using `pull_request_target`.

`runHook` hard-codes `sh -c`, which will fail on Windows where `sh` is typically unavailable (and OpenCode is cross-platform). Consider selecting the shell per-platform (e.g., `cmd.exe /d /s /c` on win32) or using `Process.run(..., { shell: true })` with appropriate escaping so hooks work consistently across OSes.

`writeIndex` / `writeEntry` attempt to write `.opencode/memory/.keep` but never ensure the directory exists. `Bun.write()` will throw `ENOENT` if `.opencode/memory` hasn’t been created yet, breaking memory sync on first use. Create the directory first (e.g., `mkdir(..., { recursive: true })`) before writing files.

Same directory-existence issue here: `writeEntry` writes `.opencode/memory/.keep` and the entry file without ensuring `.opencode/memory` exists, which can throw on first run. Ensure the directory is created before these writes.

Targeting Terminal may launch Terminal unexpectedly or fail if Terminal doesn’t support that command in a `tell` block. Use a plain `display notification ...` (or `tell application "System Events"`) instead.

The managed config link uses an absolute path from a local machine (`/Users/...`), which will be broken for readers and in GitHub rendering. Use a repository-relative link (e.g. `managed/opencode.json`) or a full GitHub URL.

`detectRepetition(...)` is called on every streamed text/reasoning delta, and it scans pattern lengths 4..200 each time over an 8KB window. This is potentially very expensive in the hot path and could slow down streaming. Consider a cheaper heuristic (e.g., only check lengths where `len * REPETITION_THRESHOLD <= tail.length`, only re-check when tail grows past a step, or maintain rolling state) to reduce per-delta work.

`MemoryExtractor.trackFix(...)` is fed `value.output.output` for every successful tool result, which can include large blobs and potentially sensitive file contents (e.g., outputs from read-like tools or commands printing secrets). Combined with `cfg.memory?.enabled !== false`, this effectively enables persistence of arbitrary tool output by default. Consider making auto-extraction opt-in by default and/or sanitizing/limiting what gets persisted (size caps, tool allowlist, redaction).

`shouldExtractMemory()` treats `memory.enabled` / `memory.auto_extract` as enabled unless explicitly `false`. That means memory extraction is effectively on by default for existing configs, which is a risky behavior change (writes to DB and `.opencode/memory` on disk). Consider defaulting to disabled unless explicitly enabled in config to avoid unexpected persistence side effects.

`maybeFlush()` can start an async `flush()` without any in-flight guard. `cleanup()` also calls `flush()` and can overlap with a background flush, causing duplicate writes or inconsistent `pending` re-queueing. Consider adding a per-session mutex/in-flight promise to serialize flushes.

These tests don’t assert any observable outcomes; they only call methods and then `cleanup()`. As written, they can pass even if `trackCommand/trackError/trackFix/...` are no-ops or broken (violates the “test must fail when bug is reintroduced” rule). Add expectations against created pending entries / store writes / filesystem output so the tests actually validate behavior.

This test will still pass if symlink creation fails (the `try { fs.symlink(...) } catch {}` swallows the error), because `evil.md` simply won’t exist and will naturally be absent from `systemPaths()`. To avoid false positives, explicitly detect whether the symlink was created and `test.skip()` (or assert) when symlinks aren’t supported/allowed on the current platform.

Same false-positive risk here: if symlink creation fails, the test still expects `alias.md` to be present even though it may not exist, but the `try/catch` makes that failure silent and the test may behave inconsistently across environments. Prefer explicitly asserting symlink support/creation and skipping the test when not available.

Same issue: if symlink creation fails, `broken.md` won’t exist and the exclusion assertion becomes meaningless. To keep the test falsifiable, confirm the symlink was created (or skip the test) before asserting behavior.
Same issue: if symlink creation fails, `sneaky.md` won’t exist and the escape-blocking assertion becomes a no-op. Verify symlink creation and skip when unsupported to avoid a test that always passes.

This config file defines `"hooks"` twice. In JSON/JSONC, duplicate keys are overwritten by the last occurrence, so the earlier `PreToolUse` hook entry (running `.opencode/hooks/guardrails.sh`) will be lost. Merge these into a single `hooks` object that contains both hook entries.

The README links to managed/opencode.json using an absolute local filesystem path (`/Users/...`). This won’t work for other developers or in GitHub. Use a repository-relative link (e.g., `managed/opencode.json`) instead.

Hooks are executed via `sh -c ...`. This will fail on Windows environments that don’t have `sh` available (and the repo previously tested on Windows in CI). Consider platform-detecting the shell (e.g., `cmd.exe /c` on win32) or using `Process.run` in a way that doesn’t assume a POSIX shell.

`process.chdir(process.env.OPENCODE_ORIGINAL_CWD)` can throw (e.g., if the directory no longer exists or is unreadable), which would crash before the app boots. Wrap this in a try/catch and either ignore failures or log a warning so the CLI remains usable.

Switching from `pull_request` to `pull_request_target` runs this workflow in the base-repo context and exposes secrets to code from untrusted forks. Since the workflow checks out and executes the PR’s code (`ref: head.sha` + `bun turbo test:ci`), a malicious PR could exfiltrate secrets. Use `pull_request` for running untrusted code, or add strict hardening (no secrets, minimal permissions, avoid executing PR code in `pull_request_target`).
```suggestion
  pull_request:
```

Same concern as test.yml: `pull_request_target` + checking out `head.sha` and running the PR code means secrets available to the workflow can be exfiltrated by a malicious fork PR. Prefer `pull_request` for typecheck, or ensure this job never has access to secrets and uses minimal permissions when using `pull_request_target`.
```suggestion
  pull_request:
```

AGENTS.md says `/test` runs the TDD workflow (RED/GREEN/IMPROVE), but `profile/commands/test.md` only describes running relevant tests (no TDD steps). Either update `/test` command docs to match the TDD workflow, or adjust this table entry so users aren’t misled.

The PR title/description focuses on adding guardrails commands/agents, but this change set also introduces substantial core OpenCode runtime changes (memory system + DB migration, hook executor/schema, notification behavior, repetition-loop compaction logic, CI workflow trigger changes, etc.). Please either update the PR description to reflect these additional behaviors or split into smaller PRs so reviewers can reason about risk and rollout separately.

`z.boolean().default(true).optional()` likely defeats the default: `optional()` short-circuits `undefined` before `default()` runs, so missing `notifications` may parse as `undefined` instead of `true`. Elsewhere in the repo, defaults are applied via `.optional().default(...)` (see config/config.ts keybind defaults). Consider using `.optional().default(true)` (or just `.default(true)` without `optional()`).

`writeIndex`/`writeEntry` write files under `.opencode/memory`, but they don’t ensure the directory exists first. Unlike `Filesystem.write(...)` used elsewhere, `Bun.write(...)` will fail if parent directories are missing. Consider `mkdir(dir, { recursive: true })` (or using `Filesystem.write`) before writing `.keep`/MEMORY.md/entries.

`detectRepetition(...)` is called on every streamed text/reasoning delta, but it scans up to 197 pattern lengths over an 8KB window and does repeated slicing/comparisons. On long streams this can add noticeable per-token overhead. Consider throttling (e.g., only check every N chars), short-circuiting earlier, or using a more incremental rolling check to reduce repeated full-window scans.

This workflow used to run unit/e2e on both Linux and Windows (matrix), but now only runs on Linux. If Windows is still a supported platform (there are win32 watcher deps in packages/opencode/package.json), dropping CI coverage risks platform-specific regressions. Consider keeping a Windows job (even if reduced scope) or documenting the support change explicitly.

The Promise returned by `this.connection.sessionUpdate(...)` inside this `.then(...)` callback is not returned/awaited, so rejections from `sessionUpdate` will bypass the following `.catch(...)` and can become unhandled promise rejections. Return/await the `sessionUpdate` call (or attach its own `.catch`) so failures are reliably logged/handled.

Same issue here: `this.connection.sessionUpdate(...)` is called inside a `.then` block but not returned/awaited, so a rejection from `sessionUpdate` will not be caught by the chained `.catch(...)`. Return the Promise (or explicitly handle `.catch` on `sessionUpdate`) to avoid unhandled rejections and lost errors.

For an invalid `modeId`, this throws a generic `Error`, while the newer config-option path uses `RequestError.invalidParams(...)`. Using `RequestError.invalidParams` here would keep JSON-RPC error codes/messages consistent for clients and avoid this being surfaced as an internal error.
